1. The frames compare one month of renting with the first month of buying. A character named Nina, who has no house yet, stands between an apartment building and a house. Beside her are two stacks of gold bars. The short stack is labeled "rent" and the tall stack is labeled "buyer's first month." The tall stack sits against the house and is much taller than the rent stack. Text on the screen says the figures are illustrative and use FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac rates. It also says "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. The scene starts as a street view with a row of houses and the title "The end of the street." It then zooms in on Nina, the apartment and the house. The stacks of gold appear and grow. A banner then shows "September 2026 average: 6.86%," which is a mortgage rate. Last, the banner "buyer's first month: $2,933" appears, with a note that all dollars are "dollars of the day." The apartment sign reads "RENT 5%," but the frames don't make clear what the 5% means.

3. It means that, at a 6.86% mortgage rate, the first month of owning costs more than the rent for a comparable place. The buyer's first month is $2,933, and the rent stack is visibly smaller. The 5% on the rent sign probably refers to rent growth, but that is my guess. The frames show the cost of the first month only. They don't show costs over time, equity, price growth or how long someone stays in the home.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that buying costs more per month than renting at today's rates. The frames don't support "rent instead of buy" or "buy instead of rent." They show only one month and carry the caption "history, not a forecast."

5. The takeaway in 4 is my own reading. The picture and text show the two stacks and the $2,933 figure, but they don't tell the viewer what to do.
